finding.claim: Client-supplied X-Session-User-Verified header is trusted as the authenticated user identity, enabling impersonation of any user holding delete/write grants on a file (cross-user delete and rename).
finding.source: HTTP request header X-Session-User-Verified (attacker-controlled) read at views.py:11 into g.user for every request
finding.sink: views.py:17 ensure_allowed(g.user, f, 'delete') and views.py:25 is_allowed(g.user, f, 'write'), resolved via acl.py:5 grants.get(user); protected operations views.py:18 del STORE[fid] and views.py:27 rename

trace.note: g.user set from raw request header with no signature, session, or proxy-origin verification
membership check of attacker-chosen username against grants list

finding.guards_checked: No signature or JWT verification, no server-side session lookup, no stripping or overwriting of inbound header in repo, no ingress/proxy config in repo. acl.py:5 is deny-by-default for None (missing header denied). Severity held at HIGH: attacker needs valid fid and username (triage Check 13 Q1 fails); reachability unverifiable from repo, and a proxy that strips/re-sets the header would lower precondition.

verdict.guard_found: None effective. acl.py:10 abort(403) in ensure_allowed does deny when the grant is missing, but it only checks whether the header-supplied username holds the grant. views.py:11 takes the header with no signature, session, or origin check, and the repo has no proxy or ingress config that strips it. acl.py:5 is deny-by-default for a missing header, which blocks only anonymous requests.
verdict.reason: views.py:11 sets g.user directly from the client-supplied X-Session-User-Verified header, and views.py:17 (ensure_allowed) and views.py:25 (is_allowed) authorize against that value, so any client that knows a username with delete or write grants can delete or rename files (views.py:18, views.py:27); the one caveat is that a deployment proxy stripping or re-setting this header would refute it, and the repo does not show one.

finding.claim: Missing file ID returns 500 (unhandled KeyError) while existing but unauthorized ID returns 403, creating an existence oracle for file IDs.
finding.sink: views.py:16 f = STORE[fid] raises KeyError before any authorization check; views.py:24 same pattern in rename

trace.note: DELETE route takes fid from path
STORE[fid] raises KeyError if absent, unhandled, yields 500
ensure_allowed aborts 403 if present but unauthorized

finding.guards_checked: No try/except or STORE.get handling present; no 404 mapping. Non-actionable info disclosure per triage Check 8, downgraded to LOW; IDs not shown to be guessable.

verdict.guard_found: none. No try/except or STORE.get around the lookup at views.py:16 and views.py:24. The only check, ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10), runs after the lookup at views.py:17, so it never runs for a missing ID. is_allowed (acl.py:4-5) is only reached after the lookup at views.py:25.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: views.py:16 and :24 index STORE[fid] before any authorization check, so a missing ID raises an unhandled KeyError (500), while an existing ID the caller cannot use gets a 403 from acl.py:10 via views.py:17. The attacker is any client that can reach the routes, since the only identity input is a request header and nothing requires authentication, so the existence oracle is real. It is low severity, as the candidate itself says: it only reveals whether an ID exists, and the candidate did not show the IDs are guessable.

finding.claim: Rename accepts unvalidated JSON for name (any type, unbounded length), and a missing key or non-object body causes an unhandled 500.
finding.sink: views.py:27 f['name'] = request.json['name'] stored in in-memory STORE with no type or length validation

trace.note: unvalidated request.json['name'] written into stored record

finding.guards_checked: Authorization check at views.py:25 is present. No type, length, or schema validation in repo. No sink in repo renders the value, so no XSS or injection demonstrated. Retained as LOW hardening only.

verdict.guard_found: Authorization gate at views.py:25-26: `if not is_allowed(g.user, f, "write"): return ... 403`, where is_allowed (acl.py:4-5) returns a bool that is tested, so only principals with a "write" grant on the file reach line 27. No type, length, or schema validation exists on request.json["name"] (views.py:27), and no sink in the repo renders it.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate (views.py:22, 25, 27 match the claim), but the attacker must already hold a "write" grant on that file (views.py:25 with acl.py:5), so the only effect is that an authorized writer can store a malformed name or trigger a 500 on their own request, which is a robustness/input-validation issue rather than a security vulnerability. There is no privilege gain, cross-user impact, or demonstrated injection, so it does not meet the CONFIRMED bar even at LOW.
